stem.text: The diagram shows an energy cycle with a series of reactions.

stem.caption: Energy cycle
stem.alt: An energy level diagram. Top level: C(s) + 1.5O2(g) + H2(g). Arrow 1 goes down from the top level to HCOOH(l) + 0.5O2(g). Arrow 2 goes down from the top level to CO(g) + H2(g) + O2(g). Arrow 4 goes down from CO(g) + H2(g) + O2(g) to CO2(g) + H2(g) + 0.5O2(g). Arrow 3 goes down from HCOOH(l) + 0.5O2(g) to the bottom level, CO2(g) + H2O(l). Arrow 5 goes down from CO2(g) + H2(g) + 0.5O2(g) to the bottom level CO2(g) + H2O(l).

stem.text: Which reactions have an enthalpy change that is an enthalpy of formation?

explanation.text: An enthalpy change of formation is for forming one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states. For each arrow, ignore the substances that are unchanged on both sides and look at what actually reacts.

Reaction 1: C(s) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g) → HCOOH(l), formation of methanoic acid. Reaction 2: C(s) + 0.5O<sub>2</sub>(g) → CO(g), formation of carbon monoxide. Reaction 5: H<sub>2</sub>(g) + 0.5O<sub>2</sub>(g) → H<sub>2</sub>O(l), formation of water (and also the combustion of hydrogen). Reactions 3 and 4 start from compounds (HCOOH and CO), so they are combustions, not formations.

optionAnalysis.text: Correct. Reactions 1, 2 and 5 each form one mole of a compound (HCOOH, CO, H<sub>2</sub>O) from its elements.
Reaction 1 is a formation, but so are reactions 2 (CO from C and O<sub>2</sub>) and 5 (H<sub>2</sub>O from H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>).
Reactions 3 and 4 are combustions of HCOOH and CO; a reactant that is already a compound cannot be part of a formation reaction.
Reactions 3 and 4 are combustions; only reaction 5 of this set is a formation.

reasoningChain: Strip each arrow down to the species that change.
1: C + O<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → HCOOH: elements → one compound, formation.

inferredMistakes.text: Missing that reaction 5 is also an enthalpy of formation of water because it is usually met as the combustion of hydrogen.
Being distracted by the spectator species (extra H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>) written on both sides of a level and misidentifying what reacts.
